name: Sara Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What is an ordinary day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, have an MBA, and lead the facilities coordination team for five buildings in a large company. Mornings start with a lift or heating complaint, then I juggle contractor slots, invoices and safety reports with my deputy Nia. I like catching a bad job before a tenant has to live with it; sitting through sales demos wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside work like just now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a nurse, and we rent while saving for a home. Our pay is steady enough and we have about four months of expenses saved; I still want any big career choice to fit the house plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the facilities coordinators the software can tidy work orders, but a roof leak still needs somebody to call the right contractor. Our company shouldn't call a neat queue a repaired building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job looks fairly secure if changes stay small; I manage five sites and people trust me when a repair goes wrong. I have roughly four months of expenses saved, and my partner's nursing pay is steady, though we still hope to buy a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday I'll keep the weekly contractor call and use the simple AI summary only after checking it against the maintenance log. In the first year of this plateau, we'll keep putting 250 a month into our house fund; I won't buy a new system just because a vendor says it's clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work. I do wish the house fund grew faster, but that's a budget question we already know how to manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you catch when you check the summary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month it marked a lift inspection complete when the contractor had only booked a visit. My deputy Nia caught it before the building manager signed the report, which is why I still read the log myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to buy a better system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a trial in one building and a price that includes staff training. My father ran a small repair firm; he taught me to pay for a tool only when it saves actual work.

say: I'd say **work orders** can be tidied by software, but someone must check whether repairs were done.
I'd keep a **contractor call** because a neat queue cannot fix a leaking roof.
think: Five sites and trusted repair judgment make my **role secure** if AI change stays small.
Four months saved and my partner's steady nursing pay support our **house plan**.
do: Check the **AI summary** against maintenance logs and keep Monday contractor calls.
Put **250 monthly** into the house fund through the first year of the plateau.
feel: I feel **calm** about work, though impatient with the house fund's pace.
S0.quote: Our company shouldn't call a neat queue a repaired building.
fieldNote: Her confidence rests on **specific errors** her team caught, not a blanket dislike of new tools.
The household has **four months saved** and a steady second income, so slow change leaves her choices intact.

steps.text: Check Monday AI summaries against the maintenance log for five sites
Add 250 monthly to the house fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say Steady Disruption will strip paperwork out of facilities management, so we should test the buying and booking tools in one site. I'd tell the coordinators to learn the system after it proves it can handle an urgent repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, budgets and contractor selection take much of my day, and software may let a regional manager cover my five sites without me. I can learn a proven tool, but typical pay and some nearby jobs don't make losing this one painless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask for a three-month trial on the east building's bookings and compare missed appointments with our current process. In the first year of steady disruption, if the trial passes, I'll take the company course on the new purchasing tool and apply to lead the repair escalation desk if my own role is merged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy when I picture a smaller management layer. I can still see a route through it if the trial shows where people remain necessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a failed trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two missed emergency callouts in three months would fail it for me, even if ordinary bookings got faster. A tenant without heat cannot wait while we admire the average score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the escalation role for less money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the pay covers our rent and lets us keep saving something toward a home. My partner and I would sit with the numbers before I accepted; pride isn't a mortgage deposit.

say: I'd support a **one-site trial** before changing purchasing and bookings across five buildings.
I'd ask coordinators to learn a **proven tool** that still handles urgent repairs.
think: A regional manager could absorb my **budget and contractor work**, leaving my role exposed.
Some nearby jobs help, but a pay cut could stall our **home savings**.
do: Trial **east-building bookings** for three months and count missed emergency calls.
Take the **purchasing course** if the trial passes; seek an escalation lead post if my role merges.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about a smaller management layer, with a possible route through it.
S1.quote: A tenant without heat cannot wait while we admire the average score.
fieldNote: Her **two-callout threshold** turns a general willingness to change into a test that staff can understand.
She would consider a new post only after a **household pay check**, showing the home goal limits her risk.

steps.text: Run a three-month booking trial in the east building and count missed callouts
Apply for repair escalation lead if her management role merges

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team AGI by 2028 puts our budget plans and contractor choices at risk before the company can settle new roles. I would ask directors for dates and a named person accountable for each site's safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nearly all my desk decisions could be cheaper in 2028; robots around 2031 don't postpone that. The nursing income and four months saved would keep our rent paid for a while, but I would not sign a house loan with my manager pay in doubt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this week, I'd pause the house search, keep the monthly 250 in cash, and ask my director which roles will remain after 2028. In the first year after AGI arrives, I'd check its contractor choices against safety rules; if my management post ends, I'd seek a facilities compliance role at another local company rather than buy a robot or start a firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, because two years is a short time to replace a career path. I'm not without help, but I can't promise my partner our house plan survives unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner we are pausing viewings, not giving up on a home. We can ask my parents to store our furniture if we ever need a smaller flat, but I would not count their spare room as our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the site if AGI makes a wrong contractor choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would insist the facilities lead signs the safety inspection after seeing the actual work. A generated approval should not become a person's injury.

say: I'd seek **dated role plans** and a named owner for each site's safety checks.
I'd tell staff our **budget and contractor choices** change with AGI in 2028.
think: My desk work faces **2028 AGI**; robots around 2031 do not extend my deadline.
Four months saved and nursing income protect rent temporarily, but our **house loan** must wait.
do: Pause **house viewings** now and keep saving 250 monthly in cash.
Check **AGI contractor choices** against safety rules after 2028; seek local compliance work if my post ends.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a short career deadline and a delayed home plan.
S2.quote: A generated approval should not become a person's injury.
fieldNote: She pauses the **house purchase** while keeping cash contributions, rather than assuming a second salary removes risk.
Her insistence on **signed inspections** follows her facilities responsibility and the 2028 thinking-work date.

steps.text: Pause house viewings while manager pay is uncertain
Keep placing 250 monthly into accessible house savings
Check AGI contractor selections against site safety rules after 2028
Apply for local facilities compliance roles if management post ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the coordinators AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn which checks cannot be skipped and to demand paid training for those who want a new role. I'd want the company to publish the plan each year, not ask us to gamble on rumors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let my partner and me build a larger deposit before making a home decision, and I could get qualified in building compliance. AGI still reaches budgets and procurement in 2031; robots in 2034 are a separate question for the repair crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beginning next year, I'd take a paid or affordable building-safety certification, after checking the fees with my partner, and keep a record of inspections I personally led. In the first year after 2031, I'd seek a compliance manager role if the company still needs one; otherwise I'd apply to the other two large employers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful, not trapped. Five years gives me enough room to earn a credential, if the training cost does not eat the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fee would make you walk away from the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the course took more than 1,000 from our savings without employer support, I'd wait and look for a cheaper route. I can defend a modest fee to my partner, not an open-ended one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspections instead of pure contract work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've already stood in boiler rooms with the maintenance leads and know how to read a report against the machine in front of us. I'd rather inspect boilers than become a buyer who never visits the site.

say: I'd seek **paid training** and yearly plans before our management work changes in 2031.
I'd tell coordinators to identify **site checks** that cannot be skipped.
think: Five years could grow our **home deposit** and give me time to qualify in compliance.
AGI reaches **budgets and purchasing** in 2031, while repair robots arrive around 2034.
do: Take **building-safety certification** next year if fees are affordable or paid, recording inspections I lead.
Seek a **compliance manager role** after 2031, locally first and then at nearby employers.
feel: I feel **watchful**, with time to qualify if training costs stay within reach.
S3.quote: I'd rather inspect boilers than become a buyer who never visits the site.
fieldNote: Her possible shift uses **real site experience** with maintenance leads, not a speculative new trade.
A **1,000 fee ceiling** guards the home deposit and makes paid training meaningful.

steps.text: Take building-safety certification next year if fees stay at most 1,000 or employer pays
Apply for local compliance management after 2031, then nearby employers if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 gives our company a full decade to train people in inspections and judgment, and employees should use it. I would ask the firm to keep apprenticeships with real site visits, not just lessons on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when thinking AI arrives, with time to pay for a home and build a compliance career first. The worry is not the date alone; it's whether I spend ten years approving contractor invoices and never gain the site experience to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep mentoring my deputy on the five-site budget and arrange one site walk each month with the maintenance lead. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stay in a compliance role if I can still inspect real work, and ask for another role if the job becomes only signing a machine's decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly calm, with a small push to get moving. A decade is a gift only if I put the site days on my calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a home before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if our deposit reaches six months of combined expenses on top of the down payment and my partner keeps steady nursing work. I won't turn a ten-year warning into a reason never to build a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your deputy learn from those walks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia would see which invoices match work that is actually done, and I'd learn where she spots a mistake before I do. My deputy Nia can catch a false invoice while I explain the boiler's broken valve.

say: I'd ask for **real site apprenticeships** while the company has a decade to prepare.
I'd tell staff to use **2036 time** for work they can show and explain.
think: At **37**, I could have a home and a compliance career before AGI reaches desk work.
Staying on **invoice approvals** alone would leave me without the site experience to move.
do: Schedule **monthly site walks** with the maintenance lead and keep mentoring my deputy this year.
Remain in **compliance work** after 2036 if inspections stay real; seek another post if reduced to signatures.
feel: I feel **mostly calm**, with a push to put site learning on the calendar.
S4.quote: My deputy Nia can catch a false invoice while I explain the boiler's broken valve.
fieldNote: The decade supports a **conditional home purchase** and deliberate growth in site-based judgment.
Her faith in apprenticeships is **practical**, grounded in what she and her deputy notice on walks.

steps.text: Keep mentoring deputy Nia on the five-site budget this year
Join the maintenance lead for one site walk each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the budget and contractor decisions could change before I earn a safety credential, and our house search would stop. A dated plan for our roles, affordable building-safety training, and a person required to sign real inspections would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is accountable after an automated contractor booking misses an emergency call. A tenant has to know whose phone will be answered.

headlineQuote: A tenant has to know whose phone will be answered.
portrait: At **27**, Sara manages facilities coordination across five buildings, using an MBA and practical site knowledge.
She and her nurse partner have **four months saved** and are building a deposit for a home.
She adopts tools after **measured trials**, counting missed emergency calls before buying a system.
Fast AGI delays the **house search**; longer runways let her qualify in building compliance and keep site work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change her budget role before she qualifies in safety and would pause the home search.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated staffing plan**, affordable training and signed safety checks would let her plan and protect tenants.
